```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  echo = FALSE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE,
  fig.align = "center", dpi = 300
)
library(tidyverse)
library(lubridate)
library(scales)
library(knitr)

fmt_p <- function(p) {
  if (p < .001) "< .001" else paste0("= ", sub("^0", "", sprintf("%.3f", p)))
}
r2 <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 2)

pay.gap <- read_csv("UK_gender_pay_gap_2025-26.csv")

n.employers <- nrow(pay.gap)
mean.gap <- mean(pay.gap$DiffMeanHourlyPercent)
sd.gap <- sd(pay.gap$DiffMeanHourlyPercent)
median.gap <- median(pay.gap$DiffMeanHourlyPercent)
min.gap <- min(pay.gap$DiffMeanHourlyPercent)
pct.favour.men <- mean(pay.gap$DiffMeanHourlyPercent > 0) * 100
pct.favour.women <- mean(pay.gap$DiffMeanHourlyPercent < 0) * 100
n.clipped <- sum(pay.gap$DiffMeanHourlyPercent < -40 |
                 pay.gap$DiffMeanHourlyPercent > 60)

gap.test <- t.test(pay.gap$DiffMeanHourlyPercent, mu = 0)
t1  <- gap.test$statistic
df1 <- gap.test$parameter
p1  <- gap.test$p.value
ci1 <- gap.test$conf.int
d1  <- mean.gap / sd.gap

pay.gap <- pay.gap %>%
  mutate(DueDate = ymd_hms(DueDate),
         Sector = ifelse(DueDate == ymd("2026-03-31"),
                         "Public Sector", "Business / Charity"))

sector.summary <- pay.gap %>%
  group_by(Sector) %>%
  summarise(n = n(),
            mean = mean(DiffMeanHourlyPercent),
            sd = sd(DiffMeanHourlyPercent),
            median = median(DiffMeanHourlyPercent),
            IQR = IQR(DiffMeanHourlyPercent),
            pct.favour.women = mean(DiffMeanHourlyPercent < 0) * 100,
            .groups = "drop")

pick <- function(col, sec) sector.summary[[col]][sector.summary$Sector == sec]
mean.pub <- pick("mean", "Public Sector");        mean.biz <- pick("mean", "Business / Charity")
sd.pub   <- pick("sd", "Public Sector");          sd.biz   <- pick("sd", "Business / Charity")
n.pub    <- pick("n", "Public Sector");           n.biz    <- pick("n", "Business / Charity")
iqr.pub  <- pick("IQR", "Public Sector");         iqr.biz  <- pick("IQR", "Business / Charity")
neg.pub  <- pick("pct.favour.women", "Public Sector")
neg.biz  <- pick("pct.favour.women", "Business / Charity")

sector.test <- t.test(DiffMeanHourlyPercent ~ Sector, data = pay.gap)
t2  <- sector.test$statistic
df2 <- sector.test$parameter
p2  <- sector.test$p.value
ci2 <- sector.test$conf.int   # Business / Charity minus Public Sector
s.pooled <- sqrt(((n.biz - 1) * sd.biz^2 + (n.pub - 1) * sd.pub^2) /
                 (n.biz + n.pub - 2))
d2 <- (mean.pub - mean.biz) / s.pooled
```

## Method

Data were taken from the UK Government's gender pay gap service for the
2025-26 reporting year. Reporting is compulsory for every UK employer with
250 or more employees, so the file is closer to a census of large employers
than to a sample of them. The analysis used the complete set of
`r comma(n.employers)` employer returns; no employer was excluded and there
were no missing values on the outcome.

The outcome was each employer's mean hourly gender pay gap, defined by the
reporting service as the difference between the male and the female mean
hourly rate, expressed as a percentage of the male rate. Positive values
therefore mean that women at that employer were paid less per hour, on
average, than men. The unit of analysis is the employer rather than the
employee: each employer contributes one value regardless of its headcount.

For the sector comparison, employers were classified using their reporting
deadline, since public sector employers were required to report by 31 March
2026 and businesses and charities by 5 April 2026.

All analyses were conducted in R. Two-tailed tests were used throughout, with
alpha set at .05.

## Results

### The overall pay gap

Across the `r comma(n.employers)` employers, the mean hourly gender pay gap
was `r r2(mean.gap)`% in women's disfavour (*SD* = `r r2(sd.gap)`,
*Mdn* = `r r2(median.gap)`%). The distribution is shown in Figure 1. It is
centred clearly to the right of parity: women were paid less per hour at
`r r2(pct.favour.men)`% of employers and more at only `r r2(pct.favour.women)`%.

```{r figure-1, fig.cap="Figure 1. Distribution of the mean hourly gender pay gap across 11,187 UK employers, 2025-26 reporting year. Positive values indicate that women are paid less per hour than men. The dashed line marks parity and the solid line the mean gap. The x axis is clipped at -40% and +60% for legibility; 121 employers fall outside this range and are retained in all analyses."}
ggplot(pay.gap, aes(x = DiffMeanHourlyPercent)) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = 0, xmax = Inf, ymin = 0, ymax = Inf,
           fill = "#C2185B", alpha = 0.05) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 2, boundary = 0,
                 fill = "#4C72B0", colour = "white", linewidth = 0.2) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed",
             colour = "grey30", linewidth = 0.6) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = mean.gap, colour = "#C2185B", linewidth = 0.9) +
  annotate("text", x = mean.gap + 1.5, y = Inf,
           label = paste0("Mean gap = ", r2(mean.gap), "%"),
           hjust = 0, vjust = 1.8, colour = "#C2185B",
           fontface = "bold", size = 3.4) +
  annotate("text", x = -1.5, y = Inf, label = "Equal pay",
           hjust = 1, vjust = 1.8, colour = "grey30", size = 3.1) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(-40, 60)) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(-40, 60, 20),
                     labels = function(x) paste0(x, "%")) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = comma, expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.08))) +
  labs(x = "Mean hourly pay gap  (positive = women paid less)",
       y = "Number of employers") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
        panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
        axis.title = element_text(colour = "grey25"))
```

A one-sample *t*-test compared the mean employer-level gap against the value
of 0% that equal average hourly pay would produce. Women at large UK
employers were paid significantly less per hour than men: the mean gap of
`r r2(mean.gap)`% was reliably greater than zero,
*t*(`r format(df1, scientific = FALSE)`) = `r r2(t1)`, *p* `r fmt_p(p1)`,
95% CI [`r r2(ci1[1])`, `r r2(ci1[2])`], *d* = `r r2(d1)`. In practical terms,
a typical large UK employer pays women about `r r2(mean.gap)` pence less for
every pound it pays men.

### Public sector versus business and charity

Descriptive statistics by sector are given in Table 1.

```{r table-1}
sector.summary %>%
  select(Sector, n, mean, sd, median, IQR, pct.favour.women) %>%
  rename(`Sector` = Sector, `N` = n, `M (%)` = mean, `SD` = sd,
         `Mdn (%)` = median, `IQR (pp)` = IQR,
         `% favouring women` = pct.favour.women) %>%
  kable(digits = 2,
        caption = "Table 1. Mean hourly gender pay gap by sector.")
```

```{r figure-2, fig.cap="Figure 2. Mean hourly gender pay gap by sector. Violins show the shape of each distribution, boxes the median and interquartile range, and white diamonds the sector means with 95% confidence intervals. The y axis is clipped at -30% and +50% for legibility; all observations are retained in the analysis."}
ggplot(pay.gap, aes(x = Sector, y = DiffMeanHourlyPercent, fill = Sector)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey30") +
  geom_violin(alpha = 0.35, colour = NA, width = 0.9) +
  geom_boxplot(width = 0.14, outlier.shape = NA, fill = "white",
               colour = "grey25", linewidth = 0.4) +
  stat_summary(fun.data = mean_cl_normal, geom = "pointrange", shape = 23,
               size = 0.6, fill = "white", colour = "grey10", linewidth = 0.7) +
  geom_text(data = sector.summary,
            aes(x = Sector, y = mean, label = paste0("M = ", r2(mean), "%")),
            inherit.aes = FALSE, hjust = -0.45, vjust = 0.4,
            fontface = "bold", colour = "grey10", size = 3.2) +
  geom_text(data = sector.summary,
            aes(x = Sector, y = -30, label = paste0("n = ", comma(n))),
            inherit.aes = FALSE, vjust = -0.4, colour = "grey45", size = 2.9) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(-30, 50)) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = seq(-30, 50, 10),
                     labels = function(x) paste0(x, "%")) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Business / Charity" = "#4C72B0",
                               "Public Sector" = "#DD8452")) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Mean hourly pay gap  (positive = women paid less)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(legend.position = "none",
        panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
        panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
        axis.text.x = element_text(face = "bold"))
```

Contrary to the expectation that public bodies would perform better, public
sector employers reported a significantly *larger* mean hourly pay gap
(*M* = `r r2(mean.pub)`%, *SD* = `r r2(sd.pub)`, *n* = `r comma(n.pub)`) than
businesses and charities (*M* = `r r2(mean.biz)`%, *SD* = `r r2(sd.biz)`,
*n* = `r comma(n.biz)`). The difference of `r r2(mean.pub - mean.biz)`
percentage points was statistically significant,
Welch's *t*(`r r2(df2)`) = `r r2(abs(t2))`, *p* `r fmt_p(p2)`,
95% CI [`r r2(-ci2[2])`, `r r2(-ci2[1])`], *d* = `r r2(d2)`. Welch's test was
used because the two groups had unequal variances.

The difference in standard deviations is not evidence of a generally wider
spread among businesses and charities. It comes from a small number of
extreme returns in that group, including the minimum value of
`r r2(min.gap)`%; the interquartile ranges were very similar
(`r r2(iqr.biz)` against `r r2(iqr.pub)` percentage points). What did differ
was how consistently the gap ran against women, which it did at all but
`r r2(neg.biz)`% of businesses and charities and all but `r r2(neg.pub)`% of
public sector employers.

## Discussion

Among large UK employers in 2025-26 there is a gender pay gap, it runs
against women, and the hypothesis of average parity can be rejected. A mean
gap of `r r2(mean.gap)`% is also a substantial difference in hourly pay, not
just a detectable one, and it is found at roughly six employers in every
seven.

Three limitations apply. The unit of analysis is the employer, so every
employer counts equally whether it employs 250 people or 250,000; this is the
mean of employer gaps rather than the gap facing the average UK worker. The
reported gap is also a raw difference in average hourly pay rather than a
measure of equal pay for equal work, so it combines unequal pay for
comparable roles with occupational segregation, meaning who occupies the
senior and the junior positions. Finally, the figures are self-reported, and
only employers with 250 or more staff are required to report, so smaller
employers are absent entirely.

The sector comparison needs one further caution. The classification rests on
the reporting deadline, which is a reliable but indirect marker of sector,
and the standardised difference between sectors is small. The conclusion to
draw is that the public sector is not the better performer here, not that it
is markedly worse.
